title.narrative: Vaccin University of Rwanda, EU-delegering MAV+ och vaccinacceptans
Vaccines University of Rwanda, EU-Delegation MAV+, and vaccine uptake

description.narrative: Contributions to strengthen capacity for vaccine development and production in Rwanda. The main contribution is the implementation of the EU's Global Gateway program Team Europe Initiative "MAV+" with the objective of strengthening capacity for vaccine development and production in Rwanda, in collaboration with the University of Rwanda and three Swedish universities, as well as a smaller program with the University of Rwanda for vaccine acceptance research.

Insatser för att stärka kapaciteten för vaccinutveckling och produktion i Rwanda. Inom ramen för insatserna ingår genomförandet av EU's Global Gateway-program Team Europe Initiative "MAV+" med målsättningen att stärka kapacitet för vaccinutveckling och produktion i Rwanda, i samarbete med University of Rwanda och tre svenska universitet, samt en mindre insats med University of Rwanda för forskning om vaccinacceptans.

Rwanda is leading efforts to transform Africas vaccine manufacturing capacity. Significant progress has been made in building infrastructure, such as Africas first mRNA vaccine manufacturing facility (BioNTech), and strengthening regulatory frameworks, including reaching WHO Maturity Level 3 of the national medical agency (RDFA) and the hosting the African Medical Agency (AMA). However, critical gaps remain in research capacity and clinical trial site maturity. Sweden, with its expertise in global health, research, and capacity strengthening, is uniquely positioned to support Rwanda in these areas. Targeted investments in research, workforce training, and clinical trial site improvement will complement ongoing donor efforts focused on manufacturing and regulatory strengthening, also part of the Team Europe Initiative (TEI) Manufacturing and Access to Vaccines, Medicines, and Health Technology Products in Africa (MAV). This holistic approach will ensure that vaccines produced in Rwanda meet international standards and address top priority diseases of the continent. Sida's contribution will be implemented by University of Rwanda (UR) in close cooperation with three Swedish universities (Karolinska Institutet, Göteborg university and Umeå University), as well as with the International Vaccine Institute (IVI), King Faisal Hospital and University of Global Health Equity. The interventions long-term goal is that Rwanda makes an important contribution to the development and manufacturing of Africa's needs of vaccines, medicines and health technologies. Rwanda and Africa at large have a severe shortage of human resources for health, science, and technology. This human resource gap creates a limitation for Rwanda to use and adapt emerging technologies that would have the potential to improve quality of life for Rwandan people, drive socio-economic development and foster sustainable growth. Vaccines are the most effective way to prevent diseases, protect against serious illness, and are safer than catching diseases, preventing millions of deaths; but only when people are vaccinated. Behavioral and social understanding of vaccine uptake, including hesitancy and practical access, is a still understudied area in Eastern Africa. In a project co-financed with Canadian IDRC, this area will be studied in Rwanda, Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda and Tanzania.
Objectives of the interventions The overall program objective is Strengthened environment for local pharmaceutical and health technologies production through research, higher education and professional skills development in Rwanda, with the following specific objectives: - Strengthened capacity of Rwanda to conduct high-quality in-country research and training in areas related to vaccines; - Upgraded clinical trial sites with capacity to conduct complex trials, including the establishment of a Center of Excellence with comprehensive infrastructure, regulatory, and training components to enable high-quality, multisite clinical trials in Rwanda; - Enhanced vaccine demand and acceptance in Eastern Africa by generating evidence on social and behavioral determinants, addressing systemic and communication barriers.
By the end of the intervention, we expect to see 7 new MSc programs and a One PhD program developed and implemented, 100 MSc and 15 PhD graduates and 3 postdocs. We expect more than 60 new peer-reviewed research publications. 4 clinical trial sites are expected to be certified and 7 to be upgraded in their quality management systems, and at least 5 cohorts of clinical trial staff to have been trained. In vaccine uptake, 15 research fellows trained and mentored over the period of 3 years and at least 200 regional researchers and practitioners will receive short training.

Strengthened capacity in research and training The main intervention of MAV was initiated in August 2024 with an inception phase, followed by the start of the full intervention in March 2025. During this period, the core partners the College of Medicine and Health Sciences at the University of Rwanda (UR), Karolinska Institutet, and the University of Gothenburg have begun to function effectively as a team, building trust, shared understanding, and coordinated ways of working. The recent visit by the main researchers from MAV at the UR to Sweden further strengthened these relationships, offering an opportunity to deepen existing collaborations, establish new ones, and transition from individual to institutional partnerships.
The project is now entering a new phase, with URs six MSc curricula and the PhD curriculum in translational health fully developed. With the accreditation of the PhD program and the MSc in Clinical Trials, all 15 PhD students, 20 MSc students, and 3 postdocs have been successfully recruited. In addition, private funding has enabled the recruitment of 5 extra PhD and 10 MSc students an unexpected and very encouraging achievement. Demand for the MSc in Clinical Trials has been particularly high, reflecting significant national needs. As a response, we are proposing to the EU to fund an additional cohort, if possible.
The remaining five MSc programs were submitted to the Higher Education Council (HEC) in February 2026 and are expected to be accredited during the spring. Following accreditation, student recruitment will begin for the next academic year, either in April or September.
In parallel, supervision training is planned for the coming year, along with a three daylong workshop on intellectual property rights (IPR), being developed by the Embassy jointly with the EUs MAV support function (TESS). Development of the MSc in Bioethics will also take place in the coming year, as part of the newly initiated collaboration with the University of Global Health Equity (UGHE).
Upgraded clinical trial sites The first steps toward strengthening Rwandas clinical trial (CT) capacity have been taken through a coordinated, evidence-based, and multi-stakeholder approach. The national clinical trial site-readiness assessment conducted by Rwanda Biomedical Center (RBC) laid the foundation for prioritizing investments under MAV, resulting in the selection of the CT sites at CHUB, CHUK and the Rwanda Military Referral and Teaching Hospital for upgrading. A three-day stakeholder workshop convened representatives from all major national institutions and international partners, leading to alignment of planned activities, a coordinated plan forward, and the definition of roles and responsibilities. The workshop also recommended establishing a steering committee and a technical working group to support coordinated implementation across institutions.
Collaboration with the International Vaccine Institute (IVI) has deepened significantly, with UR, RBC, FDA, IVI, KI, Sida, and Expertise France now working together on detailed plans for site readiness. IVI is positioned to support Rwanda in achieving internationally recognized standards, including ICHGCP and ISO accreditation, and will continue to contribute through technical assistance, Quality management systems (QMS) audits, mentorship, and its established vaccinology courses.
Regional partners such as CDT Africa and AHRI have strengthened Rwandas CT capacity by supporting curriculum review and participating in national consultations. Additional foundational activities outside MAV have further contributed to progress: RBCs site-readiness study guided MAV planning; the SANOFI/IVI/KI initiative trained 22 Rwandan professionals in CT and biomedical research through a train-the-trainer model, providing a skilled cohort ready to support MAV implementation; eligible Rwandan researchers were encouraged to apply for WHOTDR clinical trial fellowships; and a new Rwanda FDA PhD student was registered at Karolinska Institutet with EDCTP funding.
Following a mandate from the Rwanda Development Board, a multi-partner proposal for the establishment of a Center of Excellence in Clinical Trials in Rwanda, based at UGHE and King Faisal Hospital, was prepared and approved. Engagements with KFH and UGHE through the stakeholder meeting and field visits have helped build relationships and clarify future collaboration.
Overall, despite delays in some components, the clinical trial team has established solid foundations for the next phase of work.
Enhanced vaccine demand and acceptance in Eastern Africa The initiative to enhance vaccine demand and acceptance in Eastern Africa has progressed from a successful inception phase into full implementation. During the inception phase, institutional ownership was secured, internal stakeholders were aligned, and the university was positioned as a regional hub for behavioral vaccine research. This process identified key capacity gaps and helped establish both a regional research agenda and a network of engaged stakeholders. The proposal was strengthened through multiple expert workshops and a Delphi review involving specialists in gender studies, anthropology of vaccination, intersectionality, and social determinants of health, ensuring a robust conceptual foundation.
Universities from Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania formally joined Rwanda in the initiative, embedding a regionally anchored and South-South collaborative structure. Sida and the Canadian funder IDRC have jointly emphasized the need for close coordination on capacity-strengthening models, training across five countries, and scientific quality assurance.
With the full program now initiated, the Eastern Africa Hub for Behavioural and Social Science Research and Capacity Strengthening for Vaccine Uptake (EARVU Hub) held its first regional collaboration meeting. Country focal persons from all five partner countries participated, marking a key milestone in operationalizing regionally led coordination. The meeting resulted in agreement on collaboration mechanisms, confirmation of the fellowship selection processes, and clarification of national level roles. Participants validated the core governance and implementation documents for postdoctoral fellowships and small grant awards, ensuring transparency, equity, and scientific rigor.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
